summary: As Singaporeans, we would like our users to explore this regional (and possibly global) issue visually, with a combination of multimedia and scientific data in the form of satellite images. In our project, we took reference from articles that use 'Scrolly-telling', bringing in both optical satellite images as well as SAR data. Optical satellite images that show a sequence of events as the user scrolls can help to break down complex information through visualisation, and also highlight how this data can be limited by smoke and cloud cover. This is where we bring in SAR data, and why there is a need for various types of satellite information. These visualisations will culminate in learning takeaways for our users.
details:
Try out the project here: https://chewycj.github.io/sarsy-datasets/
Built for NASA Space Apps 2026, our project is a scrollytelling story about the Indonesian peatland and plantation fires that have caused haze across Southeast Asia, especially during the severe El Niño, told with optical satellite data and NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) data. As the user scrolls through the website, the story unfolds through sequences of frames from satellite data that sync with the scrolling motion, as the haze weaves through Southeast Asia, impacting communities and biodiversity in the region. It also incorporates interactive sections for users to learn more about the satellite data.

Benefits and creativity

We believe that presenting the media as a guided visual narrative is the most suitable way to bring data across clearly and concisely for the general audience. This understanding will then empower both individuals and larger stakeholders to take up action to prevent this in the future, using the data they have in hand.

An important aspect of our project is highlighting why different types of satellite observations matter. Optical imagery helps users visualise land cover and vegetation changes, while radar observations provide a complementary perspective that can capture the Earth's surface regardless of cloud cover or illumination conditions. Interactive sections allow users to explore the satellite imagery, understand radar visualisations and learn how to interpret the information.

Tools used

The project was developed as a web application using JavaScript, React+Vite, HTML and CSS, with interactive scrolling and visual components for an engaging experience. Our team worked with satellite observations from NASA and ISRO's NISAR mission, optical satellite imagery from the Copernicus Browser from ESA and JAXA's Himawari observations.

Considerations

In designing SARsy datasets, we considered how to balance scientific data with accessibility, and how to convey the limitations and complementary strengths of different satellite sensors, while retaining user engagement.

We aim to take users on a journey that helps them visualise, understand and care about the changes happening to our planet.
